summary: What a relational database is and why it is used, the key terms table, record, field (attribute) and index, and primary, foreign and composite keys.

blocks.content: An organised, structured collection of related data stored so that it can be easily **searched, sorted, updated and shared**.
A database in which data is stored in several **tables (relations)** that are **linked to each other by keys**. Each table stores data about one kind of thing (entity).

blocks.title: Why use a relational database instead of one flat file?
columns: Problem with a single flat file
How a relational database solves it
rows: **Data redundancy** — the same data is repeated in many rows
Each fact is stored **once**, in one table
**Inconsistency** — a change made in one row but not another
Hard to search and combine data
Queries (SQL) join tables and filter data quickly
Access rights per table/user; validation rules protect **data integrity**

blocks.content: A school stores student details in **Students**, course details in **Courses**, and which student takes which course in **Enrolments**. A student's address is stored once, even if they take ten courses.

items.title: Table (relation)
items.content: A set of data about **one type of entity**, arranged in rows and columns. *Students* above is a table.

items.title: Field / attribute
items.content: **One column** — one item of data stored about every entity. *FirstName, Grade.*

items.title: Record (tuple)
items.content: **One row** — all the data about one entity. *S002, Timur, Ospanov, 12, 30/11/2008.*

items.title: Index
items.content: An extra data structure that stores selected field values with pointers to records, so that searching and sorting on that field are **much faster** (like the index at the back of a book).

blocks.content: Mark-scheme definitions: "A **record** is a collection of related fields"; "A **table** is a collection of related records." Learn them word for word.
An index speeds up **searching**, but slows down inserting and updating (the index must be updated too) and uses extra storage.
A field (or fields) whose value **uniquely identifies each record** in a table. It cannot be empty and cannot repeat. *StudentID in Students.*
A field in one table that is the **primary key of another table**; it creates the **link (relationship)** between the tables. *StudentID in Enrolments.*

A primary key made of **two or more fields** together, used when no single field is unique. *(StudentID, CourseID) in Enrolments — a student can take many courses and a course has many students, but each pair appears once.*

blocks.title: Simple vs composite primary key
rows: Used when one field is unique on its own
Used when only the combination is unique

blocks.content: To explain a relationship in an exam, name **both** keys: "StudentID is the **primary key** in Students and a **foreign key** in Enrolments, which links the two tables."
